transcript:
# Day 24, Economics and Systems Thinking: Supply, demand and what prices actually do (Friedrich Hayek, 1899 to 1992; "The Use of Knowledge in Society," 1945)

Picture a supply chain manager at a bank in Delaware. One morning the price of a component she buys, say the chips that go into card terminals, jumps 20 percent. She has no idea why. Maybe a plant flooded in Malaysia. Maybe a new phone launch is soaking up capacity. Maybe a shipping lane closed. She does not know and she does not need to know. The price alone tells her what to do: order less, stretch the terminals she has, maybe look at a substitute. Thousands of people around the world make the same move the same week, and none of them talked to each other.

That is the puzzle Friedrich Hayek set out to explain in a short 1945 paper called "The Use of Knowledge in Society." Hayek was an Austrian economist who spent most of his career in London and Chicago and won the Nobel in 1974. His question sounds simple: how does an economy coordinate millions of people who each know only a tiny piece of the whole?

His answer starts with a claim about knowledge. The knowledge that matters for running an economy is not mostly scientific knowledge, the kind you can put in a textbook. It is knowledge of "the particular circumstances of time and place": the foreman who knows a machine is about to fail, the trader who knows a warehouse has empty space this week, the shop owner who notices customers stopped asking for a product. This knowledge is scattered across millions of heads, it changes constantly, and much of it cannot be written down or sent up a chain of command fast enough to be useful.

So no central planner, however smart, can gather it all. Hayek's point is not that planners are stupid. It is that the information does not exist in one place and never can.

Prices solve this. A price is a compressed signal. When tin becomes scarce, for whatever reason, its price rises. Every user of tin now has a reason to use a little less, and every potential producer has a reason to make a little more. Nobody needs to know the cause. The price carries just enough of the relevant fact, the scarcity, and strips away everything else. Hayek called the price system a kind of machinery for registering change, and he compared it to a telephone network or a set of dials that let people adjust without understanding the whole picture. Supply and demand curves, the ones from your MBA economics class, are really a picture of this: the price is where the dispersed decisions of buyers and sellers happen to meet.

Here is the strongest objection. Prices only carry good information when markets are working well. If one seller controls the market, the price tells you about its market power, not about scarcity. If a factory pollutes and nobody pays for it, the price of its product is too low and sends a false signal. And the economist Joseph Stiglitz, with Sanford Grossman, showed in 1980 that prices cannot be perfectly informative, because if they were, nobody would bother gathering information in the first place and the information would stop flowing into prices. Critics also note that Hayek's argument against central planning rests on 1945 computing. Some modern writers argue that with enough data, planning could work. Hayek's defenders answer that the problem was never computing power. It was that much of the relevant knowledge is tacit, local, and only revealed when people act on it. The 2008 crisis is a fair test case both sides claim: prices clearly misled, but a planner would have had less information, not more.

This builds on the earlier readings in this track. Opportunity cost is what a price is actually measuring. Incentives and the cobra effect showed what happens when someone sets a price or a reward from the top without knowing the local picture. Thinking at the margin is exactly what a price change nudges each person to do. And there is a link across to the Strategy track: Sun Tzu's "know the enemy and know yourself" is a claim about the value of dispersed, local information, which is Hayek's whole point.

Question for the day: at work, where is a price or a metric doing the thinking for you, and what local knowledge is it leaving out?

Primary source to look up: F. A. Hayek, "The Use of Knowledge in Society," American Economic Review, September 1945, sections 3 through 6. It is about ten pages and very readable.
